body.objective: Students will be able to analyze art about identity.
body.iCan: I can analyze art about identity.
successCriteria: I can identify how artists show identity in their work
I can interpret symbols, colour and setting in a portrait
I can plan ideas for my own identity artwork
body.hook: A self-portrait can show much more than a face. Artists include objects, colours, backgrounds and symbols to show where they come from, what they care about and how they see themselves. Before you make art about identity, you'll learn to read how other artists do it.

vocabulary.definition: The qualities, beliefs, culture and experiences that make a person who they are.

study.title: Reading Identity
study.question: How do artists express who they are?
study.passage:
Part 1, Gallery walk (15 minutes): Look at four portraits or self-portraits (shown from gallery websites), such as:
• A self-portrait with objects from the artist's daily life in the background.
• A portrait using bright, symbolic colours rather than realistic skin tones.
• A work by an Indigenous artist that combines a person with patterns, animals or land.
• A photo-collage portrait built from many images.
For each, record: What objects or symbols appear? What do colours suggest? What does the setting tell us? What might the artist want us to know?
Part 2, Identity web (10 minutes): Draw a web with your name in the middle. Add branches for family and culture, places, interests, values, challenges and goals.
Part 3, Symbol sketches (20 minutes): Choose three branches and sketch a symbol for each. For example: a mountain for growing up in Alberta, a basketball for a passion, a tree for family roots.
Privacy note: You choose what to share. Your identity artwork can show as much or as little as you're comfortable with.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images from public gallery and museum websites.
steps: Share one symbol and its meaning with a partner
discussion: Which artwork told you the most about the artist? How?
Why might an artist use symbols instead of words?
Which of your symbols is strongest, and why?
study.product: Write a plan for an identity artwork: list three symbols, explain what each means, describe your colour choices and sketch a possible composition.

examples.title: Reading a symbol
examples.problem: A portrait includes an empty chair. What might it mean?
examples.answer: It could suggest someone who is missing or a loss

examples.title: Colour and identity
examples.problem: Why might an artist paint a face in blue and gold?
examples.answer: To express feelings or ideas, such as calm and pride, rather than realism

examples.title: Context
examples.problem: Why does knowing when and where a portrait was made help?
examples.answer: It helps explain symbols and choices linked to the artist's world
examples.explore: How might your context show in your art?

examples.title: Visual metaphor
examples.problem: Show "growing up" as a visual metaphor.
examples.answer: A sprouting plant or a tree with rings
examples.explore: Think of another metaphor for change.

practice.q: Name three things to look for in a portrait.
Name three branches of an identity web.
practice.a: Family and culture, interests and values (also places, challenges, goals).

practice.q: Give an example of a personal symbol.
practice.a: A mountain for growing up in Alberta.

practice.q: Why might a portrait use unrealistic colours?
What does the privacy note say?
How many symbols do you sketch?
Why might an artist use symbols instead of words?
practice.a: Symbols can show complex ideas visually and invite interpretation.

practice.q: How can context change the meaning of a symbol?
practice.a: Symbols can mean different things in different cultures or times.

practice.q: Why is it important to respect how others choose to show identity?
practice.a: Identity is personal, and people decide what to share.

practice.q: How could composition emphasize the most important symbol?
practice.a: Place it centrally, make it larger or use contrast.

misconceptions: Thinking a portrait must look realistic
Thinking symbols have only one meaning
Feeling you must share private details
